lastText: File ClosedAnswering, Never AskingMajor DefeatWehrmacht High Command, 1940 — 1945End of hostilities: MARCH 1945 (PROJECTED) — filed late, out of sequenceImmediate AftermathThe end comes early, around March 1945 — the calendar itself the clearest casualty of this path's decisions. What surrenders at the end is less an army than a casualty ledger with a rear echelon. And it ended immobile — whatever strength remained stood where it stood, out of fuel, defending only what it could walk to. So little organized force remained by the end that both Allied advances accelerated freely — the final meeting line lands wherever logistics, not resistance, decided. Taking Malta rewrote the Mediterranean's arithmetic for the rest of the war — the one theater where a single island really was the fulcrum its advocates claimed. Sixth Army left the Volga as an army — the single largest body of men any decision in this campaign moves from the dead column to the living. The Ruhr fortress order repeated the war's oldest mistake at its largest possible scale — an intact reserve, husbanded across years, encircled with the factories it was chained to. The Bismarck never sailed — held in port rather than risked on the Atlantic breakout that historically cost the Royal Navy the Hood and cost the Kriegsmarine the ship itself within a week.
